verses.zh: 以下所记的是摩西在约旦河东的旷野、疏弗对面的亚拉巴―就是巴兰、陀弗、拉班、哈洗录、底撒哈中间―向以色列众人所说的话。
verses.en: This is what[NOTE:1] Moses said to all of Israel in the Transjordanian[NOTE:2] wilderness, the arid rift valley opposite[NOTE:3] Suph,[NOTE:4] between[NOTE:5] Paran[NOTE:6] and Tophel,[NOTE:7] Laban,[NOTE:8] Hazeroth,[NOTE:9] and Di Zahab.[NOTE:10]
notes: Heb “These are the words.”

Heb “on the other side of the Jordan.” This would appear to favor authorship by someone living on the west side of the Jordan, that is, in Canaan, whereas the biblical tradition locates Moses on the east side (cf. v. 5). However the Hebrew phrase בְּעֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן (beʿever hayyarden) is a frozen form meaning “Transjordan,” a name appropriate from any geographical vantage point. To this day, one standing east of the Jordan can describe himself as being in Transjordan.
The Hebrew term מוֹל (mol) may also mean “in front of” or “near” (cf. NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT).
This place is otherwise unattested and its location is unknown. Perhaps it is Khirbet Sufah, 4 mi (6 km) SSE of Madaba, Jordan.
The Hebrew term בֵּין (ben) may suggest “in the area of.”
Paran is the well-known desert area between Mount Sinai and Kadesh Barnea (cf. Num 10:12; 12:16).
Tophel refers possibly to eṭ-Ṭafîleh, 15 mi (25 km) SE of the Dead Sea, or to Dâbîlu, another name for Paran. See H. Cazelles, “Tophel (Deut. 1:1),” VT 9 (1959): 412-15.
Laban. Perhaps this refers to Libnah (Num 33:20).
Hazeroth. This probably refers to ʿAin Khadra. See Y. Aharoni, The Land of the Bible, 199-200.
Di Zahab. Perhaps this refers to Mina al-Dhahab on the eastern Sinai coast.
verses.commentary:
1:1 "These are the words" This is the Hebrew title for the book. The Hebrew VERB "spoke" (BDB 180, KB 210,
Piel PERFECT) is a COGNATE to the NOUN "words" (BDB 182). Because the book itself says that
these are the words of Moses, I believe that this excludes the possibility that this is entirely the work of a later redactor, editor, or
compiler. We actually have the words of Moses, which in reality are the words of YHWH (e.g. Deut. 7:4; 11:13-14; 17:3; 29:6). This is
not to say that there are not some editorial additions or that Moses recorded his own death. But the bulk of the material and the theology are Mosaic.

Similar phrases seem to divide Deuteronomy into sections:

- "These are the words," Deut. 1:1 (1:1-5, introduction to first sermon)

- "This is the law," Deut. 4:44 (4:44-49, introduction to second sermon)

- "This is the commandment," Deut. 6:1

- "These are the words of the covenant," Deut. 29:1 (start of third sermon)

- "This is the blessing," Deut. 33:1

While I am commenting on this controversial issue of authorship/date, let me state clearly that I believe all
Scripture is inspired (cf. 2 Tim. 3:15-17). The issue of authorship and date are hermeneutical issues, not inspiration issues! The
Holy Spirit is the divine author of all canonical texts. Is this pre-suppositional? Absolutely! But it is a crucial presupposition,
which must be reviewed and studied before any exegesis of Scripture has validity. The doctrines of Inspiration and Canonization
are the twin pillars on which an authoritative Bible rests!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSES' AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH, II

SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM (J.E.P.D.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "which Moses spoke" There were a large number of people who left Egypt with Moses and it would have
been physically impossible for him to speak to all of them at one time. Possibly he spoke to the elders and then they repeated
it to smaller groups or this is a literary way of denoting a written document.

▣ "to all Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "across the Jordan" This possibly means "in the region of" (BDB 719). The next two sentences are very
specific as to the geographical location of the camp of Israel when Moses gave them this revelation. It became an idiom for

- the area east of the Jordan (cf. Num. 35:14; Deut. 1:1,5; 4:41,46,47,49)

- the western area (cf. Deut. 3:20,25; 11:30; 9:1)

It requires additional phrases to clarify which bank of the river is meant (cf. R. K Harrison, Introduction to
the Old Testament, pp. 636-638).

▣ "the wilderness" This is not desert but uninhabited pasture land (BDB 184), where the grass is dry and dead most
of the year except in winter and early spring.

▣ "the Arabah" This is literally "arid plains" (BDB 787). This refers to the Jordan Valley (i.e. the Great Rift
Valley) which goes from the Sea of Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba (really from Turkey to Mozambique). So, it refers to the area
both to the south (modern usage) and to the north of the Dead Sea and we are not certain exactly which part is meant. It
can refer to the east bank of the Jordan (cf. Deut. 3:17; 4:49) or the west bank (cf. Deut. 11:30). Verse 1 is a summary of the
Israelites' trek from Egypt to Sinai.

▣ "Suph" This (Egyptian loan word) is literally "reeds" (BDB 693). This can refer either to salt
water plants (cf. 1 Kgs. 9:26; Jon. 2:5) or more commonly fresh water plants (cf. Exod. 2:5). Here it can be translated "area of reeds"
or the city of Suph and may relate to Deut. 1:40 (literally, "yom suph, "sea of reeds"), which was translated
"Red Sea" by the LXX

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE RED SEA

▣ "Paran" The term "paran" (BDB 803) can refer to a wilderness area which was north of the wilderness
of Sinai, but south of the wilderness of Judea (cf. Num. 13:3,26). The oasis of Kadesh-Barnea was located in this wilderness
area.

However, in this verse Paran seems to be an unknown location (possibly a city) on the eastern bank of the Jordan.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WILDERNESSES OF THE EXODUS

▣ "Topel" The term means "whitewash" (BDB 1074). This is an unknown site, but is apparently on the
eastern side of the Jordan in the territory of Moab.

▣ "Laban" This is one of several campsites of Israel in Sinai. The term means "white" (BDB 526 III). This
is an unknown site. Some scholars place it on the route from Sinai to Moab (cf. Libnah of Num. 33:20-21), while
others make it a city or village on the eastern bank of the Jordan in Moab.

▣ "Hazeroth" It is this place name (BDB 348) that has caused scholars to assert that the locations
mentioned after "Arabah" are Israel's camp locations between Mt. Sinai and the plains of Moab (cf. Deut. 1:2). If so,
Laban would be Libnah (cf. Num. 33:20-21) and Hazeroth would refer to Num. 33:17-18. This was the site where
Aaron and Miriam murmured against Moses' leadership or his new marriage to a Cushite woman (cf. Numbers 12).

▣ "Dizahab" This name (BDB 191) is a combination of Aramaic "place of" and Hebrew "gold."
The rabbis related this to the Egyptians giving the Israelites gold when they left Egypt (cf. Exod. 3:22; 11:2; 12:35),
but in context, this was a place name. The site is unknown. It was either

- on the east bank of the Jordan in Moab and thereby close to the other places mentioned

- on the route from Mt. Sinai to Moab

verses.zh: （从何烈山经过西珥山到加低斯・巴尼亚有十一天的路程。）
verses.en: Now it is ordinarily an eleven-day journey[NOTE:1] from Horeb[NOTE:2] to Kadesh Barnea[NOTE:3] by way of Mount Seir.[NOTE:4]
notes: An eleven-day journey was about 140 mi (233 km).
Horeb is another name for Sinai. “Horeb” occurs 9 times in the Book of Deuteronomy and “Sinai” only once (33:2). “Sinai” occurs 13 times in the Book of Exodus and “Horeb” only 3 times.

Kadesh Barnea. Possibly this refers to ʿAin Qudeis, about 50 mi (80 km) southwest of Beer Sheba, but more likely to ʿAin Qudeirat, 5 mi (8 km) NW of ʿAin Qudeis. See R. Cohen, “Did I Excavate Kadesh Barnea?” BAR 7 (1981): 20-33.
Mount Seir is synonymous with Edom. “By way of Mount Seir” refers to the route from Horeb that ended up in Edom Cf. CEV “by way of the Mount Seir Road”; TEV “by way of the hill country of Edom.”
verses.commentary:
1:2 "eleven days journey from Horeb. . .Kadesh-barnea" This verse may be a summary of the movement of
Israel from Mt. Horeb/Sinai to the oasis at Kadesh, but if so, it does not fit well between Deut. 1:1 and 3. This may have
been included to show that the journey should have taken eleven days, but because of unbelief (cf. Num. 13-14) it took a whole
generation (38 years plus). This eleven-day trip seems to confirm the site of Mt. Horeb/Sinai as in the southern tip of the
Sinai Peninsula.

Notice that the place of the giving of the law is called "Horeb." Horeb is a Hebrew word for "waste"
or "desolate" (BDB 352, KB 349). Sinai (BDB 696) is a non-Hebrew word. The two terms are used synonymously. However,
it is possible that "Horeb" refers to a mountain range in the southern Sinai peninsula and "Sinai" refers to the highest
peak. They refer to the place where Moses brought Israel to meet YHWH (e.g. Horeb, Exod. 3:1; Deut. 1:6,19; 4:10,15;
5:12 and Sinai Exod. 19; Lev. 7:38; 25:1; 26:46; 27:34; Num. 1:1,9; 3:1,4,14; 9:1,5).

Why the name "Horeb" is used most often in Deuteronomy (except Deut. 33:2) and "Sinai" most often
in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers is unknown. There is literary variety in the writings of Moses. This could refer to:

- Moses using different scribes

- changes by later scribes for unknown reasons

- literary variety

- normal variations involving oral traditions (see Walton, D. Brent Sandy, The Lost World of Scripture)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS (The Route, III.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LOCATION OF MT. SINAI

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOREB

▣ "Mount Seir" BDB 973 says the term "Seir" can mean

- goat

- hairy

- hairy as in well-wooded with trees

- KB 1989 asserts that it means "hairy"

In the OT this term is associated with the mountainous region of Edom (cf. Gen. 14:6; 36:20-21,30;
Deut. 1:2,44; 2:1,4-5; 33:2). It is often characterized as a mountain (cf. Gen. 14:6; 36:8-9; Deut. 2:1). Therefore, originally it was
a Horite mountainous area annexed by Edom.

▣ "Kadesh-barnea" This is a large oasis on the border of Edom (cf. Num. 20:16), about 50 miles south of
Beersheba, with four natural springs.

Its name has two elements. The first is from the Hebrew for "holy" (BDB 873). The
second is unknown. It became the hub of their wilderness wanderings (cf. Numbers 13-14) for 38 yeras until the
unbelieving generation died. Both Miriam and Aaron died here (cf. Num: 20:1,2b).

verses.zh: 出埃及第四十年十一月初一日，摩西照耶和华藉着他所吩咐以色列人的话都晓谕他们。
verses.en: However, it was not until[NOTE:1] the first day of the eleventh month[NOTE:2] of the fortieth year[NOTE:3] that Moses addressed the Israelites just as[NOTE:4] the Lord had instructed him to do.
notes: Heb “in” or “on.” Here there is a contrast between the ordinary time of eleven days (v. 2) and the actual time of forty years, so “not until” brings out that vast disparity.
The eleventh month is Shebat in the Hebrew calendar, January/February in the modern (Gregorian) calendar.
The fortieth year would be 1406 b.c. according to the “early” date of the exodus. See E. H. Merrill, Kingdom of Priests, 66-75.
Heb “according to all which.”
verses.commentary:
1:3 "the fortieth year" This is the only date in Deuteronomy. "Forty" (BDB 917) is used so often in the Bible that
it seems to refer to a long, indefinite period of time. The actual chronology seems to be 38 years (from Sinai to the plains of Moab).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

SPECIAL TOPIC: DATE OF THE EXODUS

▣ "on the first day of the eleventh month" The author is making every effort to locate the place
and time of these words to Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANCIENT NEAR EASTERN CALENDARS

▣ "Moses spoke to the children of Israel, according to all that the Lord had
commanded him to give to them" YHWH is the author; Moses is the channel, but all these commands come
from the covenant-making God.

There is great variety in the names for Deity in Moses' writings. The following is an example from Deuteronomy 1-4.

- The Lord (YHWH), Deut. 1:3,8,27,34,37,41,42,43,45; 2:12,14,15,17,21,31;
3:2,20,21,26 (twice); 4:12,14,15,21,27

- The Lord (YHWH) our God (Elohim), Deut. 1:1,19,20,25,41; 2:29,36,37; 3:3; 4:7

- The Lord (YHWH) your God (Elohim), Deut. 1:10,21,26,30,31,32; 2:7(twice),30;
3:18,20,21,22; 4:2,3,4,10,19,21,23 (twice),24,25,29,30,31,34,40

- The Lord (YHWH), the God (Elohim) of your fathers, Deut. 1:11,21; 4:1

- God (Elohim), Deut. 1:17; 2:33; 4:24 (jealous God), 31(compassionate God), 32,33

- Lord (Adon) God (YHWH), Deut. 3:24

- Lord (YHWH), my God (Elohim), Deut. 4:5

- Lord (YHWH), He is God (Elohim), Deut. 4:35,39

There has been much speculation about this variety:

- multiple authors

- multiple scribes

- theological distinctives

- literary variety

OT scholars must admit that the authorship, compilation, editing, and scribal activity connected
to the Canonical books of the OT is a mystery. We must be careful to not let our modern western literary theories
or our a-priori theological assumptions demand one and only one interpretation. Mystery means mystery.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. and D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSES' AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH

SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM (J.E.P.D.)

verses.zh: 那时，他已经击杀了住希实本的亚摩利王西宏和住以得来、亚斯他录的巴珊王噩。
verses.en: This took place after the defeat[NOTE:1] of King Sihon[NOTE:2] of the Amorites, whose capital was[NOTE:3] in Heshbon,[NOTE:4] and King Og of Bashan, whose capital was[NOTE:5] in Ashtaroth,[NOTE:6] specifically in Edrei.[NOTE:7]
notes: Heb “when he struck [or “smote”].”
See Deut 2:26-3:22.
Heb “who lived.”
Heshbon is probably modern Tell Hesban, about 7.5 mi (12 km) south southwest of Amman, Jordan.
Heb “who lived.”
Ashtaroth is probably Tell ʿAshtarah, about 22 mi (35 km) due east of the Sea of Galilee.
Edrei is probably modern Derʿa, 60 mi (95 km) south of Damascus (see Num 21:33; Josh 12:4; 13:12, 31).
verses.commentary:
1:4

NASB NRSV, JPSOA
"after he defeated"

NKJV, Peshitta
"after he had killed"

TEV
"after the Lord had defeated"

NJB
"He had defeated"

LXX
"after he had struck"

The VERB (BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil INFINITIVE) means
"to smite" with the grammatical and theological implication is that it was YHWH. He is the first cause and only cause
(i.e. Isa. 14:24-27; 45:7; Amos 3:6)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

▣ "Sihon" Sihon (BDB 695) was the Amorite king of a region next to Og, king of Bashan, on the
eastern side of Jordan. Moses was commanded by God (cf. Deut. 2:4-9) not to attack the Israelites' relatives of Moab
and Edom (Lot's descendants by his own daughters, cf. Gen. 19:30-38). The only other route to the Jordan was
through Sihon's kingdom. The capital city of Heshbon was the first major city that the Israeli army conquered
(cf. Deut. 2:26-37; Num. 21:21-32).

▣ "Og" Og (BDB 728) was the Amorite king of this region called Bashan, which had two large cities (cf. Josh. 12:4)
and many villages (cf. Deut. 3:1-10). He was apparently one of the Rephaim (giants, cf. Deut. 3:11) who inhabited
Canaan (cf. Deut. 2:20; Josh 12:4). It was the descendants of these giants (cf. Deut. 2:11) at Hebron who had caused
Israel to reject the two faithful spies' report (cf. Num. 13:22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DATE OF THE EXODUS

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

▣ "Astaroth" This city (BDB 800) was named after the female consort of the Canaanite fertility
god Baal. She was called Asherah or Astarte in Canaan. Because of the mentioning of Rephaim, it is
possible that this city is referenced in Gen. 14:5.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "Edrei" This was one of the capital cities of Og (BDB 204, cf. Josh. 12:4; 13:12).

verses.zh: 摩西在约旦河东的摩押地讲律法说：
verses.en: So it was in the Transjordan, in Moab, that Moses began to deliver these words:[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “this instruction”; KJV, NIV, NRSV “this law”; TEV “God’s laws and teachings.” The Hebrew noun תּוֹרָה (torah) is derived from the verb יָרָה (yarah, “to teach”) and here it refers to the Book of Deuteronomy, not the Pentateuch as a whole.
verses.commentary:
1:5 "in the land of Moab" This is where the Israelites camped before entering the Promised Land. It is
the location just north of the Dead Sea on the eastern bank of the Jordan, where Deuteronomy was written.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB

▣ "Moses undertook" This VERB (BDB 383, KB 381, Hiphil PERFECT)
implies "volitional commitment" (cf. Gen. 18:27; Exod. 2:21; Jdg. 19:6).

▣ "to expound this law" This VERB (BDB 91, KB 106, Piel PERFECT)
means to "make clear" or "understandable." This word only appears here and two other times where it is translated "write"
(cf. Deut. 27:8; Hab. 2:2). Instruction which is not clear or understandable is useless and, in this covenantal context, dangerous.

The term "law" (i.e. torah, BDB 435) is the Hebrew term for "teaching" or "instruction"
(cf. Deut. 4:8,44; 27:3,8,26; 28:58,61; 29:20,28; 30:10; 31:9,11,12; 32:46). In this context it refers to Moses' sermons
delivered to Israel on the eastern side of Jordan across from Jericho, on the plains of Moab, just before the
Israelites crossed the Jordan without him.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR GOD'S REVELATION, II. B.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAWS IN THE ANE

verses.zh: 「耶和华―我们的　神在何烈山晓谕我们说：你们在这山上住的日子够了；
verses.en: The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb and said, “You have stayed[NOTE:1] in the area of this mountain long enough.
notes: Heb “lived”; “dwelled.”
verses.commentary:
1:6 "Lord" This is the unique name for the covenant God of Israel (i.e. YHWH, BDB 217,
cf. Gen. 2:4). It is used of God as Savior, Redeemer, and covenant-making God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "our God" The personal PLURAL PRONOUN implies a covenant relationship, initiated
and accepted at Sinai. This is the name of Deity, "Elohim" (BDB 43). It is used of God as Creator, Provider, and
Sustainer of all creation (e.g. Gen. 1:1-2:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY C.

▣ "Horeb" See note at Deut. 1:2 and
SPECIAL TOPIC: LOCATION OF MT. SINAI.

▣ "'You have stayed long enough at this mountain'" YHWH now tells the people it is time for them to
do what He initially had commanded them, occupy Canaan (cf. Gen. 15:13-21; Numbers 13-14)! They had stayed at
Mt. Horeb for about one year (compare Exod. 19:1 with Num. 10:11).

verses.zh: 要起行转到亚摩利人的山地和靠近这山地的各处，就是亚拉巴、山地、高原、南地，沿海一带迦南人的地，并黎巴嫩山又到幼发拉底大河。
verses.en: Head out[NOTE:1] and resume your journey. Enter the Amorite hill country, and all its neighboring areas, including the rift valley,[NOTE:2] the hill country, the foothills,[NOTE:3] the Negev,[NOTE:4] and the coastal plain—all of Canaan and Lebanon as far as the Great River, that is, the Euphrates.
notes: Heb “turn”; NAB “Leave here”; NIV, TEV “Break camp.”

As a geographic feature the rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba. The reference here probably includes the Jordan Valley and continues to the wider part of the rift valley below the Dead Sea. Some versions transliterate the name as Arabah (ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV).

The שְׁפֵלָה (shephelah) is the geographical region between the Mediterranean coastal plain and the hill country, sometimes called the “western foothills” (NIV, CEV, NLT), “Judean foothills” (HCSB), “lowland” (NASB, ESV), or by the Hebrew “Shephelah” (NRSV).

The Negev is the area of central, southern Judah, south of the hill country and Beer Sheba and west of the rift valley. As a geographic feature it is a depression extending south to the gulf of Aqaba, but the reference here is probably to the northern portion of the region.
verses.commentary:
1:7

NASB
"Turn and set your journey"

NKJV
"Turn and take your journey"

NRSV
"Resume your journey"

TEV
"Break camp and move on"

JPSOA
"Start out and make your way"

LXX
"turn, and depart"

The first VERB (BDB 815, KB 937, Qal IMPERATIVE) means
"turn," but is used in several senses:

- turn to look at something/someone, Exod. 2:12; 16:10; Num. 12:10

- turn so as to change direction, Gen. 18:22; 24:49; Exod. 14:25; 21:33; Deut. 1:7,24; 2:3; 9:15; 10:5

- turn to other gods, Lev. 19:4; Deut. 29:18; 30:17; 31:18,20

- seek help from, Lev. 19:31; 20:6

- the approach of

- evening, Deut. 23:11

- morning, Exod. 14:27

The second VERB (BDB 652, KB 704, Qal IMPERATIVE) means
"pull out," "pull up," or "set out," which is used often in Numbers for the Israelites moving their camp site. This
usage continues in Deuteronomy (e.g. 1:7,19,40; 2:1,24). It originally referred to pulling up the tent stakes.

▣ "and go" This is the third parallel Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 97, KB 112).

▣ There are five topological divisions of Palestine running north to south mentioned:

- "in the hill country of the Amorite" ‒ This refers to the eastern bank of the Jordan and
the kingdoms of Sihon and Og.

- "in the Arabah" ‒ This refers to the Jordan rift valley south of the Dead Sea (BDB 787,
cf. Deut. 1:1,7; 2:8; 3:17; 4:49; 11:30; Josh. 8:14; 11:2,16; 12:3; 18:18)

- "in the hill country and in the lowlands" ‒ This refers to the area west and south of the Dead
Sea, later to become the tribal allocation of Ephraim and Judah.

- "the Negev" ‒ This is the arid desert land south of the Dead Sea and to the west (BDB 616)

- "by the seacoast" ‒ This is the coastal plain running from Egypt to Lebanon (i.e. Shephelah, BDB 410)

All of these taken together refer to the land promised to Abraham in Genesis 15.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GEOGRAPHICAL DIVISIONS OF THE PROMISED LAND

verses.zh: 如今我将这地摆在你们面前；你们要进去得这地，就是耶和华向你们列祖亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各起誓应许赐给他们和他们后裔为业之地。」
verses.en: Look! I have already given the land to you.[NOTE:1] Go, occupy the territory that I,[NOTE:2] the Lord, promised[NOTE:3] to give to your ancestors[NOTE:4] Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to their descendants.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “I have placed before you the land.”
Heb “the Lord.” Since the Lord is speaking, it is preferable for clarity to supply the first person pronoun in the translation.
Heb “swore” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT). This refers to God’s promise, made by solemn oath, to give the patriarchs the land.
Heb “fathers” (also in vv. 11, 21, 35).
Heb “their seed after them.”
verses.commentary:
1:8 Verse 8 is a series of commands:

- "See" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "Go in" ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "Possess" ‒ BDB 439, KB 441, Qal IMPERATIVE

▣ "'I have placed the land before you'" The Hebrew term for "have placed" is the same as "given"
(BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT). YHWH was now giving them the land as He had promised
Abraham (Gen. 12:1, line 5; 15:12-21; Exod. 6:8), but they had to possess it. Notice the conditional aspect of
even this foundational covenant (e.g. Deut. 4:1; 5:33; 6:18; 8:1; 16:20; 30:16,19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "possess the land" See SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣ "the land which the Lord swore to give to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac,
and to Jacob" See Deut. 4:37; 6:10; 9:5; 10:11,15; 30:20; Gen. 12:5-7; 13:14-17; 15:18; 26:3; Exod. 32:13; 33:1. This
land would include the area from Kadesh-Barnea in the south to Byblos and Zephan, Zedad and Lebo-hamath in the
north (possibly even as far east as the head waters of the Euphrates, cf. Gen. 15:18). See MacMillan Bible Atlas, p. 47.

There are several places where the general boundaries of the Promised Land are given (Exod. 34:1-12;
Deut. 1:6-8; 3:12-20; 11:24; Josh. 1:3-4). It was only during David's and Solomon's reigns that this whole general area was under Israel's control.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

verses.zh: 「那时，我对你们说：『管理你们的重任，我独自担当不起。
verses.en: I also said to you at that time, “I am no longer able to sustain you by myself.
verses.commentary:
1:9 "at that time" This is a recurrent phrase in Deuteronomy. The first four chapters are a review of
YHWH's gracious acts on Israel's behalf. This idiom is a way of denoting a past act (cf. Deut. 1:9,16,18; 2:34; 3:4,8,12,18;4:14).

▣ "I am not able to bear the burden of you alone" There are two possibel references.

- Exodus 18:13-26 for Jethro's advice to Moses about this very problem (i.e. Moses being the only judge)

- Numbers 11:12-14 where Moses uses these very words to describe the problems associated with trying to govern Israel

verses.zh: 耶和华―你们的　神使你们多起来。看哪，你们今日像天上的星那样多。
verses.en: The Lord your God has increased your population[NOTE:1] to the point that you are now as numerous as the very stars of the sky.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “multiplied you.”
Or “heavens.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
verses.commentary:
1:10 "the Lord your God has multiplied you" This was part of YHWH's promise
to the Patriarchs (e.g. Gen. 13:16; 17:2,20; 22:17; 48:4; Lev. 26:9; Deut. 7:13).

▣ "as the stars of heaven" This phrase is also found in Gen. 15:5; 22:17; 26:4; Exod. 32:13; Deut. 10:22;
28:62. Other parallel phrases used to portray uncountable numbers (cf. Gen. 16:10) of Israelites are: "dust of the earth"
(cf. Gen. 12:1; 13:16; 28:14; Num. 23:10); and "sand of the sea" (cf. Gen. 22:17; 32:12). All of these from a man who
was childless until age 100 (i.e. Abraham)!

In Deut. 1:28 the Israelites, who are more numerous than the stars, are afraid of the inhabitants
of Canaan because of their:

- numbers

- size

- walled cities

What irony!

See full note at Gen. 13:16.

verses.zh: 惟愿耶和华―你们列祖的　神使你们比如今更多千倍，照他所应许你们的话赐福与你们。
verses.en: Indeed, may the Lord, the God of your ancestors, make you a thousand times more numerous than you are now, blessing you[NOTE:1] just as he said he would!
notes: Heb “may he bless you.”
verses.commentary:
1:11 "the God of your fathers" This often repeated designation asserts that the same God who spoke
to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is still active in the lives and destiny of their descendants.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "increase you a thousand-fold" This is obviously an idiomatic phrase. The number 1,000
was a multiple of ten (times 3) and, therefore, a symbol of greatness or numerousness (cf. Ps. 90:4; 2 Pet. 3:8). Here is a
list of hyperbolic usages from NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 417:

- the work of God in blessing, Deut. 1:11; Job 42:12; Ps. 144:13

- military blessing, Josh. 23:10

- military curse for unbelief, Deut. 32:30; Isa. 7:23; 30:17; Amos 5:3

- enduring sovereignty of God, Ps. 90:4

- God's covenant promises, Deut. 7:9; Ps. 105:8

- God's wrath vs. God's love, Exod. 34:7; Deut. 5:9-10

- blessing of being in God's temple, Ps. 84:10

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

verses.zh: 但你们的麻烦，和管理你们的重任，并你们的争讼，我独自一人怎能担当得起呢？
verses.en: But how can I alone bear up under the burden of your hardship and strife?
verses.commentary: 1:12 "strife" This means "lawsuit" (BDB 936).

verses.zh: 你们要按着各支派选举有智慧、有见识、为众人所认识的，我立他们为你们的首领。』
verses.en: Select wise and practical[NOTE:1] men, those known among your tribes, whom I may appoint as your leaders.”
notes: The Hebrew verb נְבֹנִים (nevonim, from בִּין [bin]) is a Niphal referring to skill or intelligence (see T. Fretheim, NIDOTTE 1:652-53).
verses.commentary:
1:13 "Choose" This VERB (BDB 396, KB 393) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. Notice
that Moses was commanding the people (i.e. their leaders) to take responsibility (they choose) for the community
along with himself (Moses appoints). These new judges (i.e. tribal leaders) were to be:

- "wise" ‒ (BDB 314) meaning capable of thoughtful and godly choices (e.g. Joseph, Gen. 41:33,39; military leaders,
Exod. 18:21; David, 2 Sam. 14:20; Solomon, 1 Kgs. 2:9; 3:12; 5:21)

- "discerning" ‒ (BDB 106, KB 122, Niphal PARTICIPLE) meaning someone who
has discretion, discernment, and intelligence (e.g. Joseph, Gen. 41:33; negative in Jer. 4:22)

- "experience" ‒ (BDB 393, KB 390, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE). This is a common
word with a large semantic field.

- NASB, TEV, NJB, JPSOA ‒ experienced

- NKJB ‒ knowledgeable

- NRSV, REB ‒ reputable

- JB ‒ tested

- NIV ‒ respected

- NET ‒ known

SPECIAL TOPIC: HE CHOSE US, I. B.

▣ "I will appoint them" The VERB (BDB 962, KB 1321) is a Qal IMPERFECT,
used in the sense of a COHORTATIVE. Moses set or appointed these chosen men to places of leadership
and judgment (e.g. Exod. 1:11; 18:21; Deut. 17:14,15; Jdg. 11:11). However, in reality, it was YHWH who "took"
(BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERFECT with waw, Deut. 1:15) them, which denotes God's choice
(e.g. Deut. 4:20,34; 1 Kgs. 11:37). The human process followed a divine plan!

verses.zh: 你们回答我说：『照你所说的行了为妙。』
verses.en: You replied to me that what I had said to you was good.

verses.zh: 我便将你们各支派的首领，有智慧、为众人所认识的，照你们的支派，立他们为官长、千夫长、百夫长、五十夫长、十夫长，管理你们。
verses.en: So I chose[NOTE:1] as your tribal leaders wise and well-known men, placing them over you as administrators of groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, and also as other tribal officials.
notes: Or “selected”; Heb “took.”
verses.commentary:
1:15 "leaders of thousands, and of hundreds, of fifties and of tens" These divisions later became the
names of military units (cf. Exod. 18:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

▣

NASB
"leaders"

NKJV, LXX
"officers"

NRSV, TEV
"officials"

NJB
"scribes"

REB, Peshitta
"commanders"

JPSOA
"heads"

This term (BDB 1009) originally referred to a scribe (i.e. one who organizes), but this does not seem to fit its
usage in Deut. 1:15; 20:5,8,9; or Josh. 1:10,32. In this context it seems to refer to a lesser judge or military helper to tribal leaders.

The UBS Handbook for Translators on Deuteronomy says, "they appear with elders (Num. 11:16) and
with judges (Deut. 16:18; Josh. 8:33), and also in military contexts (Deut. 20:5,8,9; Josh. 1:10; 3:2)" p. 26.

verses.zh: 「当时，我嘱咐你们的审判官说：『你们听讼，无论是弟兄彼此争讼，是与同居的外人争讼，都要按公义判断。
verses.en: I furthermore admonished your judges at that time that they[NOTE:1] should pay attention to issues among your fellow citizens[NOTE:2] and judge fairly,[NOTE:3] whether between one person and a native Israelite[NOTE:4] or a resident foreigner.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “you.” A number of English versions treat the remainder of this verse and v. 17 as direct discourse rather than indirect discourse (cf. KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).
Heb “brothers.” The term “brothers” could, in English, be understood to refer to siblings, so “fellow citizens” has been used in the translation.

The Hebrew word צֶדֶק (tsedeq, “fairly”) carries the basic idea of conformity to a norm of expected behavior or character, one established by God himself. Fair judgment adheres strictly to that norm or standard (see D. Reimer, NIDOTTE 3:750).

Heb “between a man and his brother.” The first use of “brother” in this verse refers broadly to fellow citizens. This second use is narrower, being in opposition to the “resident foreigner.” The גֵּר (ger) “resident foreigner” was not simply a foreigner (Hebrew נֵכָר; nekar) but was essentially a naturalized citizen and had equal protection under the law. This is one of the verses designed to ensure that equal treatment (see also Deut 10:16-19; 16:18-20; Exod 12:49; Num 15:16, 29).
On the Hebrew ger (גֵּר) “resident foreigner,” see notes at Exod 12:19 and Deut 29:11.
verses.commentary:
1:16-17 Moses charged these new tribal judges to be impartial (cf. Deut. 16:19; 24:17). Impartiality is a
characteristic of God (cf. Deut. 10:17). Israel was meant to be a people and society that revealed the character of
YHWH so that the world would come to place their trust and faith in Him. Since the Fall (i.e. Genesis 3) this has
been God's plan. Israel failed, but the ideal Israelite (i.e. Jesus, cf. Gen. 3:15; Isaiah 53) succeeded (e.g. John 14:5-7, 8-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

1:16 "alien" Non-Jews (lit. "sojourners" or "resident aliens," BDB 158) were to be treated as equals in the legal realm
(cf. Lev. 19:33-34,35). Israel was to deal with them graciously (cf. Lev. 23:22; Deut. 10:19; 14:29; 24:14,17,19-21; 27:19). Israel had
been aliens in Egypt (cf. Exod. 22:21; 23:9; Deut. 10:18-19) and knew how it felt!

▣ "righteously" See SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

verses.zh: 审判的时候，不可看人的外貌；听讼不可分贵贱，不可惧怕人，因为审判是属乎　神的。若有难断的案件，可以呈到我这里，我就判断。』
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] must not discriminate in judgment, but hear the lowly[NOTE:2] and the great alike. Nor should they be intimidated by human beings, for judgment belongs to God. If the matter being adjudicated is too difficult for them, they should bring it before me for a hearing.
notes: Heb “you,” and throughout the verse (cf. NASB, NRSV).
Heb “the small,” but referring to social status, not physical stature.
verses.commentary:
1:17 "You shall not show partiality in judgment" The term "partiality" is literally "face" (BDB 815). The
VERB (BDB 647, KB 699, Hiphil IMPERFECT) means "to regard." The point being
that as a person approached the judge, the judge should not attempt to see or recognize who it was coming before
him, but to hear the case fairly and impartially. The judge was to treat all cases without prejudice (cf. Lev. 19:15).

▣ "You shall not fear man" This VERB (BDB 158 III, KB 185, Qal IMPERFECT)
means "dread" or "awe." In this context "dread" is demanded. In Deuteronomy this term is used in two contexts. God's
leaders/judges are not to fear the reactions of men to their decisions (Deut. 1:17) and God's people are not to fear the
messages of false prophets (Deut. 18:22).

This term is used often in the Psalms to express the covenant believer's respect and awe of YHWH
(e.g. Deut. 33:8; 22:23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

▣ "The case that is too hard for you, you shall bring to me" Moses was YHWH's representative to the
people (i.e. "judge"). He was also seen as a prophet (cf. Deut. 1:18; 18:15-22).

verses.zh: 那时，我将你们所当行的事都吩咐你们了。」
verses.en: So I instructed you at that time regarding everything you should do.

verses.zh: 「我们照着耶和华―我们　神所吩咐的从何烈山起行，经过你们所看见那大而可怕的旷野，往亚摩利人的山地去，到了加低斯・巴尼亚。
verses.en: Then we left Horeb and passed through all that immense, forbidding wilderness that you saw on the way to the Amorite hill country as the Lord our God had commanded us to do, finally arriving at Kadesh Barnea.
verses.commentary:
1:19-25 "Then we set out" The VERB (BDB 652, KB 704, Qal IMPERFECT
with waw) is regularly used of the Exodus (cf. Exod. 12:37; 13:20; 14:15; 16:1; and often in Numbers 33). These
verses relate to the journey from Mt. Sinai to Kadesh-barnea.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOCATION OF MT. SINAI

1:19 "Horeb" The two titles of the sacred mountains, Horeb and Sinai, are used synonymously. Horeb is a
Semitic term. Sinai is not semitic but possibly relates to the Wilderness of Sin. Sin is a term for a small desert
plant common in the region. Some believe that Horeb is the mountain range and Sinai is the peak, but we don't really
know for certain. See full note at Deut. 1:2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOREB

▣ "that great and terrible wilderness" Usually the term "wilderness" (BDB 184) means uninhabited
pastureland, but this trek took them across the desert of the Sinai Peninsula. There were few sources of natural
water. YHWH provided water and food for them supernaturally during this forty year period. Today, this desert is
called Et Tih, which means "the wandering." This journey was about 100 miles and crossed very rough country (i.e. Deut. 8:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WILDERNESSES OF THE EXODUS

▣ "the hill country of the Amorites" This would refer to the southern part of the land of Canaan (i.e. Negev, Arabah).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GEOGRAPHICAL DIVISIONS OF THE PROMISED LAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

▣ "just as the Lord our God had commanded us" For the names for Deity see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C. and D. YHWH led them by

- Moses' words

- the Shekinah cloud of glory, which rested over the tabernacle. When it moved Israel followed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CLOUD. . .THE PILLAR

▣ "we came to Kadesh-barnea" The Hebrew word for holy is kadosh (BDB 871), from which we
get "Kadesh." Kadesh-barnea means "holy" or "separated," possibly "holy city," "holy place, or "separated place." It was
an important campground for the Israelites as it was for Abraham because it was the largest oasis in the area
(i.e. about 50 miles south of Beer-sheba) in the wilderness of Paran (LXX of Num. 33:36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY

verses.zh: 我对你们说：『你们已经到了耶和华―我们　神所赐给我们的亚摩利人之山地。
verses.en: Then I said to you, “You have come to the Amorite hill country, which the Lord our God is about to give[NOTE:1] us.
notes: The Hebrew participle has an imminent future sense here, although many English versions treat it as a present tense (“is giving us,” NAB, NIV, NRSV) or a predictive future (“will give us,” NCV).
verses.commentary:
1:20-21 These verses have caused problems for commentators because of the change in usage between
the PRONOUNS "our" and "your," which is common throughout the book of Deuteronomy. This is
one reason why some believe that Deuteronomy was written by several people. I think that Moses wrote (or dictated)
the majority of the revelations, but it is obvious that his writings have been edited by later scribes and may contain
the comments of the original scribe or later scribe.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOSAIC AUTHORSHIP OF THE PENTATEUCH

SPECIAL TOPIC: LATER SCRIBAL ADDITIONS, II.

verses.zh: 看哪，耶和华―你的　神已将那地摆在你面前，你要照耶和华―你列祖的　神所说的上去得那地为业；不要惧怕，也不要惊惶。』
verses.en: Look, he[NOTE:1] has placed the land in front of you![NOTE:2] Go up, take possession of it, just as the Lord, the God of your ancestors, said to do. Do not be afraid or discouraged!”
notes: Heb “the Lord your God.” The pronoun (“he”) has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons, to avoid repetition.
Or “has given you the land” (cf. NAB, NIV, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
1:21 "See, the Lord your God has placed. . .take possession" This may be a
reference to Deut. 1:8, where YHWH, through Moses, told the people to possess the land which He had promised
to the Patriarchs (cf. Deut. 12:5-7; 13:14-17; 15:18; 26:3).

This verse, like Deut. 1:7 and 8, contains several commands:

- "See" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "Go up" ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "Take possession" ‒ BDB 439, KB 441, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "Do not fear" ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "Be dismayed" ‒ BDB 369, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: POSSESS THE LAND

▣

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA
"Do not fear or be dismayed"

NKJV
"do not fear or be discouraged"

TEV
"do not hesitate or be afraid"

NJB, REB
"do not be afraid or discouraged"

Peshitta, LXX
"fear not, neither be terrified"

This prohibition from YHWH was based on their trust in His covenant promises and presence! This
phrase occurs twelve times in the OT (e.g. 31:8; Josh. 1:9; 8:10; 10:25; 1 Chr. 22:13; 28:20; 2 Chr. 20:15; 32:7; Jer. 30:10; 46:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

verses.zh: 你们都就近我来说：『我们要先打发人去，为我们窥探那地，将我们上去该走何道，必进何城，都回报我们。』
verses.en: So all of you approached me and said, “Let’s send some men ahead of us to scout out the land and bring us back word as to how we should attack it and what the cities are like there.”
verses.commentary:
1:22 Numbers 13:1-3 is the background for this verse. It recalls Moses' commands to the tribes:

- "Send" ‒ BDB 1018, KB 1511, Qal COHORTATIVE

- "Search out" ‒ BDB 343, KB 340, Qal IMPERFECT, used in a JUSSIVE sense

- "Bring back" ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

verses.zh: 这话我以为美，就从你们中间选了十二个人，每支派一人。
verses.en: I thought this was a good idea,[NOTE:1] so I sent[NOTE:2] twelve men from among you, one from each tribe.
notes: Heb “the thing was good in my eyes.”
Or “selected” (so NIV, NRSV, TEV); Heb “took.”
verses.commentary:
1:23 "I took twelve of your men, one man for each tribe" Moses was smart to try and include each of the
tribes so that each one felt included.

verses.zh: 于是他们起身上山地去，到以实各谷，窥探那地。
verses.en: They left and went up to the hill country, coming to the Eshcol Valley,[NOTE:1] which they scouted out.
notes: Or “the Wadi Eshcol” (so NAB).sn The Eshcol Valley is a verdant valley near Hebron, still famous for its viticulture (cf. Num 13:22-23). The Hebrew name “Eshcol” means “trestle,” that is, the frame on which grape vines grow.
verses.commentary:
1:24 "the valley of Eshcol" This term (BDB 79) means "cluster" or "stalk." Numbers 13:23-24 says that
they cut one cluster of grapes that was so big that it took two men to carry it on a pole. This is how the valley
(or Wadi) got its Hebrew name, but its location in southern Palestine is uncertain, possibly somewhere close
to Hebron (cf. Num. 13:22,23).

▣ "spied it out" "Spied" (BDB 920, KB 1183, Piel IMPERFECT with waw) is a
variation of the word for "foot" (BDB 919), which implies that they walked through the land. They had no
animals to ride and it was a real step of faith for them to walk throughout this land and be seen by its inhabitants.

verses.zh: 他们手里拿着那地的果子下来，到我们那里，回报说：『耶和华―我们的　神所赐给我们的是美地。』
verses.en: Then they took[NOTE:1] some of the produce of the land and carried it back down to us. They also brought a report to us, saying, “The land that the Lord our God is about to give us is good.”
notes: The Hebrew text includes “in their hand,” which is unnecessary and somewhat redundant in English style.
verses.commentary:
1:25 "It is a good land which the Lord our God is about to give us" What a
powerful covenantal affirmation! Yet, they did not act on the theological affirmation, but on their fear (e.g. Deut. 1:21).

verses.zh: 「你们却不肯上去，竟违背了耶和华―你们　神的命令，
verses.en: You were not willing to go up, however, but instead rebelled against the Lord your God.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “the mouth of the Lord your God.” To include “the mouth” would make for odd English style. The mouth stands by metonymy for the Lord’s command, which in turn represents the Lord himself.
verses.commentary:
1:26 "rebelled" The VERB (BDB 598, KB 632, Hiphil IMPERFECT
with waw) becomes a common word in Deuteronomy (e.g. 1:26,43; 9:7,23,24; 21:18,20; 31:27; and also in the
Psalms). Its COGNATE in Aramaic means "to dispute with" and in Syriac, "to contend with." It denotes willful,
known disobedience!

▣ "the command of the Lord" The command in Deut. 1:8 and 21 were for
them to go up and take the land. The account of the spies and their report is found in Numbers 13.

verses.zh: 在帐棚内发怨言说：『耶和华因为恨我们，所以将我们从埃及地领出来，要交在亚摩利人手中，除灭我们。
verses.en: You complained among yourselves privately[NOTE:1] and said, “Because the Lord hates us he brought us from Egypt to deliver us over to the Amorites so they could destroy us!
notes: Heb “in your tents,” that is, privately.
verses.commentary:
1:27 "you grumbled in your tents" The people were in their tents grumbling (BDB 920, KB 1188, Niphal
IMPERFECT with waw); they were not doing it publicly, but God saw their hearts (cf. Ps. 106:25) and knew that
they were rebelling against Him (i.e. "slanderous whispers," cf. Prov. 16:28; 18:8; 26:20,22). God knows not only what
we say (cf. Deut. 1:25c), but what is in our heart-our motives (cf. Num. 14:1-6; 1 Sam. 2:3; 16:7; 1 Kgs.8:39; 1 Chr. 28:9;
2 Chr. 6:36; Ps. 7:9; 44:21; 94:11; 139:1-4; Prov. 15:11; 20:27; 21:2; Jer. 11:20; 17:9-10; 20:12; Luke 16:15; Acts 1:24;
15:8; Rom. 8:26; 1 John 3:20; Rev. 2:23).

▣ "the Lord hates us" In this verse the people are impugning the motives
and nature of YHWH (e.g. Deut. 9:28). They had forgotten all of the wonderful promises and provisions of God during their
trek from Sinai to Kadesh and had started focusing on their present situation, which they viewed as devastating.

verses.zh: 我们上哪里去呢？我们的弟兄使我们的心消化，说那地的民比我们又大又高，城邑又广大又坚固，高得顶天，并且我们在那里看见亚衲族的人。』
verses.en: What is going to happen to us? Our brothers have drained away our courage[NOTE:1] by describing people who are more numerous[NOTE:2] and taller than we are, and great cities whose defenses appear to be as high as heaven[NOTE:3] itself! Moreover, they said they saw[NOTE:4] Anakites[NOTE:5] there.”
notes: Heb “have caused our hearts to melt.”
Heb “greater.” Many English versions understand this to refer to physical size or strength rather than numbers (cf. “stronger,” NAB, NIV, NRSV; “bigger,” NASB).
Or “as the sky.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.
Heb “we have seen.”

Heb “the sons of the Anakim.”sn Anakites were giant people (Num 13:33; Deut 2:10, 21; 9:2) descended from a certain Anak whose own forefather Arba founded the city of Kiriath Arba, i.e., Hebron (Josh 21:11).
verses.commentary:
1:28 "Our brethren have made our hearts melt" The people tried to blame the spies for their unbelief. The
term "melt" (BDB 587, KB 606) is imagery for a person becoming fearful and losing the will to resist (cf. Deut. 20:8;
Josh. 2:11; 5:1; 7:5; and possibly 14:8).

▣

NASB, REB
"bigger and taller"

NKJV, Peshitta
"greater and taller"

NRSV, TEV, NJB, NIV, JPSOA
"stronger and taller"

NET
"more numerous and taller"

LXX
"great and numerous"

It is obvious from the different translations that the question is about the first term. Is it
synonymous or does it add new information?

The ADJECTIVE (BDB 152) basically means "great." It is used of:

- great in extent

- great in number

- great in intensity

- great in importance

The term is common and has a wide semantic field. Only context can clarify its
meaning. The Septuagint seems to understand these terms as "more populous and mightier" (as does the
UBS Text Project, p. 267, but with considerable doubt, a "C" rating). Part of the problem of translation is
the place of "giants" in the OT!

verses.zh: 并且你们的妇人孩子，就是你们所说、必被掳掠的，和今日不知善恶的儿女，必进入那地。我要将那地赐给他们，他们必得为业。
verses.en: Also, your infants, who you thought would die on the way,[NOTE:1] and your children, who as yet do not know good from bad,[NOTE:2] will go there; I will give them the land and they will possess it.
notes: Heb “would be a prey.”

Do not know good from bad. This is a figure of speech called a merism (suggesting a whole by referring to its extreme opposites). Other examples are the tree of “the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen 2:9), the boy who knows enough “to reject the wrong and choose the right” (Isa 7:16; 8:4), and those who “cannot tell their right hand from their left” (Jonah 4:11). A young child is characterized by lack of knowledge.
verses.commentary:
1:39 "your little ones who you said would become a prey" This refers to Numbers 14:3,31. Because of the
adults' disbelief YHWH is telling them that their children surely would inherit the land just as He had promised.

▣ "who this day have no knowledge of good or evil" Historically this is referring to the children who
came out of Egypt. YHWH did not hold them responsible until they were capable of covenant understanding and commitment (e.g. Isa. 7:15).

In this text two sides/poles can be seen in:

- "I will give it to them" (God's sovereignty, cf. Deut. 1:8)

- "They shall posses it" (human choice and responsibility, cf. Deut. 1:8)

Heb “the Reed Sea.” “Reed” is a better translation of the Hebrew סוּף (suf), traditionally rendered “red.” The name “Red Sea” is based on the LXX which referred to it as ἐρυθρᾶς θαλάσσης (eruthras thalassēs, “red sea”). Nevertheless, because the body of water in question is known in modern times as the Red Sea, this term was used in the translation. The part of the Red Sea in view here is not the one crossed in the exodus but its eastern arm, now known as the Gulf of Eilat or Gulf of Aqaba.

body of water crossed early in the Exodus, unless it means "in the general direction of."
